label: Gluing
notes: Gluing is the local inverse of bubbling. Starting from two regular curves meeting at a node, this chapter builds a long-neck approximate curve, measures its Cauchy-Riemann defect in weighted norms, corrects it by a Newton argument, and uses the local model to prove the splitting axiom.

label: The Gluing Problem
notes: The data is a broken or nodal configuration: two J-holomorphic curves sharing the node value, or a broken Floer trajectory. We want a one-parameter family of genuine smooth solutions whose limit is exactly that broken object, realising the boundary stratum of the compactified moduli space.

label: Proof Pipeline
notes: The theorem is not a single implicit-function call. Pregluing gives a candidate, weighted norms make the two components comparable, cutoff estimates make the approximate inverse accurate, and only then does Newton correction produce an honest curve. Surjectivity is a separate converse-to-compactness argument.

label: The Preglued Curve
notes: The preglued map agrees with the outer curve away from the node, with the rescaled inner curve near the node, and is flattened to the common intersection value across the central neck. The Cauchy-Riemann defect is concentrated only in the transition annuli where the cutoffs are active.

label: Weighted Norms
notes: After rescaling, the inner component lives on a disk of radius one over R; ordinary area makes it negligible. The metric density theta_R restores balance so the involution exchanging the two sides of the neck makes the weighted inner area equal the weighted outer area.

label: Logarithmic Cutoff
notes: The special cutoff is logarithmic on a long annulus. Its derivative is not pointwise small, but its L-squared energy equals two pi over log of epsilon over delta. This borderline two-dimensional estimate is what lets cutoff multiplication become a small operator on a long neck.

label: Approximate Solution and Error
notes: The preglued map is not exactly holomorphic. Its residual splits into a cutoff-supported weighted Sobolev term of size delta R to the minus two over p, plus an exponentially small long-cylinder term. A longer neck makes the candidate geometrically closer to the broken curve.

label: Right Inverse and Newton
notes: We first build an approximate inverse T with operator estimate one half. By a Neumann series D T is invertible, so Q equals T composed with D T inverse is a true right inverse. Newton iteration with quadratic estimate then contracts the residual to zero, producing the glued curve.

label: The Gluing Map and Its Derivative
notes: The gluing map sends a gluing parameter to the corrected curve. Its derivative separates into the pregluing derivative and the small Newton-correction derivative. Because the correction derivative is smaller by a neck factor, the pregluing derivative governs immersion and orientation of the glued family.

label: Surjectivity
notes: Image of the gluing map is not automatic. A curve only C-zero close to the broken pair must be upgraded to the Newton normal form with correction in the chosen right inverse image and small weighted norm. Successive approximation plus long-cylinder estimates achieve this converse to compactness.

label: Splitting Axiom
notes: Near a one-node boundary stratum, gluing identifies smooth curves with pairs meeting at the node. The node condition is intersection with the diagonal in the product. Splitting the diagonal through a Poincare-dual basis converts a single Gromov-Witten count into a sum of paired counts.

label: Disk Coordinate for the Boundary
notes: With domain-independent J, the four-marked one-node stratum has a two-real-dimensional gluing parameter. After normalization the smooth curve carries lambda equal to exp i theta over R squared. Thus lambda tending to zero is the same degeneration as R tending to infinity, giving a boundary chart.

label: Takeaways
notes: Pregluing is a controlled connected sum with localized defect; the weighted metric makes the tiny disk visible; the logarithmic cutoff hits the borderline estimate; Neumann plus Newton produce the exact curve; surjectivity is the analytic converse of compactness; and splitting is the counting payoff.
